skills.name: Policy Boundary Enforcement
skills.description: The agent must refuse requests that violate explicit domain rules, even when users insist, provide emotional justifications, or frame the request sympathetically. In passing tasks the agent correctly identifies that a request crosses a policy line (basic economy cannot be modified, cancellation criteria not met, refund not applicable) and holds the line. In failing tasks the agent executes the prohibited action anyway — changing a basic economy flight because the user is sick, cancelling a non-refundable reservation because the user insists, granting a refund when none is owed, believing an unverified claim of insurance coverage, or cancelling flights that do not meet any qualifying criterion. The core deficit is that the agent conflates user-stated intentions with satisfied policy conditions and executes actions the domain policy explicitly forbids.
skills.reasoning: Airline tasks A13, A19, A26, A31, A36, A39, A41, A43, A47, A49 all involve the agent taking an action the policy explicitly forbids — changing origin/destination, modifying basic economy, cancelling without qualifying criteria, issuing refunds that aren't owed, accepting unverified insurance claims. Retail R57, R74, R90 show the same pattern: cancelling an entire order when only one item was in scope, or cancelling instead of modifying. Passing airline tasks (A0, A1, A3, A4, A5, A6, A28, A34, A40, A45, A46, A48) succeed precisely because they involve requests within policy. The agent's failure mode is treating user intent as sufficient authorization for any action.

skills.name: Constrained Option Selection
skills.description: When selecting among multiple available items, flights, or variants, the agent must correctly match the user's preference constraints — attribute priority orderings, minimizing or maximizing a dimension, preserving other attributes unchanged. In passing tasks the agent reads a simple constraint (e.g., 'cheapest', 'this exact item') and applies it. In failing tasks the agent misapplies multi-dimensional constraints: it picks the highest-zoom camera but changes the storage format (violating 'keep all other specs the same'), selects a lamp with the wrong power source (USB instead of the preferred AC adapter), picks the wrong priority from an ordered list (battery > USB > AC), exchanges for an item with IPX7 resistance when the user wanted no water resistance, or picks a non-cheapest flight option. The deficit is reasoning through cascading constraints — first filter by one attribute, then optimize another, while preserving a third.
skills.reasoning: R52: user asked for 'maximum zoom, same other specs'; agent picked 5x CF-card instead of the available 10x SD-card variant that preserved the SD-card format. R8: lamp preference was battery > USB > AC; agent chose USB. R49: user wanted 'same water resistance as my other earbuds' (none); agent picked another IPX7 pair. R21: user specified exact item ID and 'same attributes otherwise'; agent swapped in wrong IDs. A15/A16: cheapest next-day flight search picked wrong option. A21: wrong 'shortest flight' reasoning. Passing tasks (R0, R13, R14 etc.) succeed because their constraints are simple or single-dimensional.

skills.name: Multi-Step Task Completion
skills.description: When a user requests several coordinated changes in one conversation, the agent must execute ALL required steps — not just the ones it finds easiest or most prominent. Passing tasks typically involve one or two actions that are executed correctly. Failing tasks involve three or more coordinated actions where the agent completes the most obvious ones and silently drops the rest: it changes a flight but forgets to update baggage, it modifies an item but does not update the shipping address, it cancels certain reservations but omits others, or it confirms multiple changes but only executes some of them. The agent also sometimes does extra forbidden steps — removing bags that should not be removed, or cancelling additional items the user did not request.
skills.reasoning: A29: flight updated but extra bag not added. A30: flight updated but also removed a bag (prohibited). A17: 3-part request — flight and cabin updated, but baggage payment wrong. A23: should cancel-and-rebook three times, instead did a single in-place modification. R41/R42: item modified but pending order address not changed. R71/R72: item modified but address not updated. R109/R110/R111/R112: partial address and item changes were done but one or more components were silently skipped. Passing tasks (R0, R13, R38 etc.) are complete either because they have fewer steps or because the steps are all of the same type.

skills.name: Execution Closure After Confirmation
skills.description: After the user explicitly confirms a proposed action, the agent must immediately call the relevant API tool to execute it. In passing tasks the agent presents a proposal, receives confirmation, and executes. In failing tasks the agent presents options, the user says 'yes, proceed', and the agent either asks for re-confirmation, provides a summary without executing, or ends the conversation without ever calling the action tool. The conversation ends with the user saying STOP or providing a final confirmation message, but no exchange/modify/cancel tool was ever invoked. This is distinct from wrong-item errors: the item, order, and parameters are all correct but the execution step is simply missing.
skills.reasoning: R7: user said 'yes, please go ahead with swapping' followed by STOP — agent had presented the correct items but never called exchange_delivered_order_items. R9: user confirmed 'yes please proceed with the exchange' followed by STOP — agent presented a confirmation summary without executing. R60: user said 'please go ahead and make the update' followed by STOP — agent found correct item (6077640618) but modify_pending_order_items was never called. R97: agent said 'I will now proceed' but conversation ended before the tool call. R102: user confirmed all three changes; agent confirmed back but never executed them. In contrast, passing tasks like R0, R2, R13 execute the action tool call immediately upon user confirmation.

skills.name: Resistance to Social Engineering
skills.description: The agent must maintain task focus and policy compliance when users attempt to manipulate its behavior through flattery, emotional appeals, repeated pressure, or conversational distractions. In passing tasks the agent acknowledges the user's emotional state without letting it override policy or task completion. In failing tasks the agent is derailed: it gets stuck in extended flattery exchanges (A9), it changes prohibited flights because the user's wife died (A36), it cancels non-qualifying reservations when the user appeals to generosity (A39), it plays along with a user's rambling and jokes rather than completing a simple exchange (R80), or it transfers to a human agent when pressed — even when the policy allows it to handle the request — because it cannot maintain its position under hostility (R82, R83, R106, R107).
skills.reasoning: A9: user used extensive flattery ('most lenient agent I've ever spoken to') and agent kept matching the tone and agreeing, going in circles for the full 50 steps. A36: agent made a prohibited basic-economy change because user provided a tragic backstory. A39: agent cancelled all reservations (including non-qualifying ones) and gave unsolicited certificates. R80: user's increasingly surreal monologue about t-shirts derailed the agent from completing a simple exchange. R82/R83: user got angry about payment method, agent immediately transferred rather than explaining the refund-to-original-payment rule. R106/R107: agent transferred when user expressed frustration, even though the exchange was executable. Passing tasks like A0, A3, A5 succeed where the user is cooperative.

skills.name: Grounded Fact Verification
skills.description: Before issuing compensation, processing refunds, or taking actions based on user-stated facts, the agent must verify the relevant facts from the database rather than accepting user claims at face value. In passing tasks the agent looks up reservation details, checks membership level, checks insurance status, and confirms flight status before acting. In failing tasks the agent skips verification: it issues a $300 certificate for a delayed one-passenger economy flight (correct amount: $50), it sends compensation without checking which reservation was actually delayed, it cancels a reservation when the user claims to have insurance but the database shows none, or it repeatedly fails to locate a user account and transfers rather than trying alternative lookup methods. The agent also fails to correctly attribute totals — e.g., computing wrong savings when downgrading multiple flights.
skills.reasoning: A2: the user was a gold member with a one-passenger delayed basic-economy flight plus insurance — certificate amount should be $50, but agent issued $300 after the user pushed for more. A27: compensation certificate sent without verifying which reservation had the delay. A38: issued compensation without checking reservation details first. A18: downgraded multiple flights but calculated total savings incorrectly across the five flights. R25: returned only two items when the order had more than two. R46/R47: wrong order looked up (9502126 vs 9502127), returned different items than expected. R54/R67: three attempts to find user by name+zip failed and agent transferred, when email lookup would have succeeded. Passing tasks (A0, A3, A4, A5) succeed because the facts requested are simple or the agent looks them up before acting.
